opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core intuition is that benchmark performance and economic value aren't linearly related. Benchmarks tend to measure capability on fairly narrow, well-specified tasks, and they often have a ceiling: once a model gets from, say, 80 to 90 percent on some test, it looks like a modest improvement. But economically, that last stretch can matter enormously.

Think about what it takes for a system to actually substitute for human labor on a job. A job isn't a single task; it's a bundle of many tasks, and you often need reliability across essentially all of them before you can hand the job over. If a model can do 90 percent of the subtasks but fails unpredictably on the remaining 10 percent, you still need a human in the loop, and the value captured is limited. Closing that gap, going from "mostly capable" to "reliably capable across the whole bundle," can unlock a discontinuous jump in value, even though on a benchmark it registers as a few points.

There's also a complementarity point. Many tasks in the economy are bottlenecked by the weakest link. When AI clears those bottlenecks, the value isn't just the value of that one task; it's the value of everything that was being held up by it. So small improvements in capability at the margin can have outsized effects on output.

And then there's scale. Once a capability crosses the threshold where it's deployable, you can run it across millions of instances at low marginal cost. Human labor doesn't scale like that. So the economic impact depends not just on how good the model is per task, but on how many copies you can run and how cheaply, which compounds with improvements in hardware and inference efficiency.

Finally, I'd point to feedback loops. If AI starts contributing meaningfully to R&D, including AI research itself, and to producing more compute, then the growth in economic value could feed back into further capability gains. That's a dynamic you just don't see by looking at a leaderboard. So I'd expect the economic curve to look much steeper than the benchmark curves might naively suggest, especially once we cross certain reliability and generality thresholds.

r001.rationale: The response explains that moving from mostly capable to reliably capable across a whole job can unlock a disproportionate jump in economic value, even when benchmark gains are small.

r002.rationale: It discusses deploying AI at scale and low marginal cost, but does not explain how a larger user base spreads fixed investment costs across more users.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing here is that the mapping between what we measure on benchmarks and what the system is actually worth economically is really nonlinear. Benchmarks tend to track something like the fraction of problems a model gets right, and that number creeps up fairly smoothly. But the economic value of a system often depends on crossing thresholds, on being reliable enough that you can actually hand a task off and not check the work.

So think about what it means to automate a task end to end. If a model gets ninety percent of the steps right, that might be almost worthless, because you still need a human sitting there supervising, and the human is the expensive part. Go from ninety to ninety-nine and suddenly you can remove the human from the loop entirely, and the value jumps by much more than the ten percent improvement in accuracy would suggest. On the benchmark that looks like modest progress. In the economy it looks like an entirely new capability.

There's also a related point about task length. We've been tracking how long the tasks are that models can complete autonomously, and that's been roughly doubling every several months. But the value of a system that can do an hour of work versus eight hours of work versus a week of work isn't linear in time, because the longer horizons are where the really valuable work lives. Coordinating a project, running an experiment, doing a piece of research. So even if the underlying capability improvement is steady and exponential, the economic value you unlock as you cross into those longer horizons can grow faster still.

And then the final piece is complementarity and scale. Once a system is good enough to be deployed, you can run it in parallel at enormous scale, and you can combine it with tools and other systems in ways that compound. So a fairly small step in measured performance can translate into a large step in what the economy as a whole can do. That's why I'm somewhat skeptical of people who look at benchmark curves and say progress is slowing or incremental. The measurements may be incremental while the economic consequences are anything but.

r001.rationale: The response explains that moving from 90% to 99% reliability can remove human supervision and make economic value jump far more than benchmark performance suggests.

r002.rationale: It mentions deploying systems in parallel at enormous scale, but does not explain that a growing user base spreads fixed investment costs across more users.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between how well an AI performs on a benchmark and how useful it is in an actual production process. There’s no reason to expect those to move proportionally.

Suppose a system can complete each step of a task with 90 percent reliability. That sounds quite good, but if you need it to complete twenty steps correctly, its reliability on the whole task can be quite low. Improving performance on each step can therefore make a much bigger difference to whether you can delegate the entire task. You might go from having something that requires constant supervision to something that can operate fairly independently.

And the economic value depends on that supervision requirement. If someone has to check everything the model does, you’re still paying for a lot of human time. Once it becomes sufficiently reliable, you can potentially deploy it much more widely.

So a relatively modest improvement in measured performance could cross a threshold that makes a whole category of work economical to automate. That’s one reason I wouldn’t interpret a slowing rate of benchmark improvement as necessarily implying a slowing rate of growth in economic value.

r001.rationale: The response explains how modest performance gains can cross an automation threshold and sharply increase economic value, but it does not connect this effect to approaching human-level performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a growing user base, fixed investment costs, or spreading those costs across users.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that measured performance and economic value aren’t the same thing. A benchmark might tell you what fraction of tasks a model can solve, but it doesn’t tell you how valuable those tasks are, or whether the model is reliable enough to use in a business.

Suppose an AI gets a little better at each step of a task that requires ten steps. That can produce a much larger improvement in its ability to complete the whole task successfully. And once it crosses a threshold where you can delegate that task without constantly checking its work, its economic usefulness can increase quite sharply.

There’s also the fact that businesses need time to figure out how to use these systems. Better tools, integration with existing workflows, and changes in how work is organized can all increase the value you get from a model even if its benchmark performance hasn’t changed much.

So I wouldn’t expect a smooth, one-to-one relationship. Relatively modest improvements in measured capabilities could unlock quite substantial economic value.

r001.rationale: The response describes modest capability improvements unlocking substantial economic value, but it does not connect that effect to approaching human-level performance.

r002.rationale: It mentions business integration and workflow changes, but not a growing user base spreading fixed investment costs across more users.
